messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert, a 67-year-old hotel manager, was mugged three months ago in the parking lot after a late shift. As he unlocked his car, a man smelling strongly of alcohol grabbed him from behind, shouted something unintelligible, and slammed his head against the door before snatching his wallet and disappearing into the night. The sound of his own skull hitting metal—a dull, percussive crack—still rings in Robert’s ears at odd moments. What stayed with him most, though, was the humiliation: a seasoned manager who prided himself on reading people and maintaining order had been reduced to a helpless victim on the ground, his dignity stripped away in seconds.

In the weeks that followed, Robert found the world had changed. He had always been a practical man, but now he caught himself scanning every face that entered the hotel lobby. People couldn’t be trusted—that was the lesson the mugging had etched into him. The stranger had looked ordinary, and then he had attacked. Robert began to believe that danger lurked behind every ordinary interaction, that the world was simply a dangerous place now and he had been naive to think otherwise. This conviction of permanent threat made him constantly watchful. At his desk, he sat with his back to the wall. In the elevator, he positioned himself near the control panel. His hypervigilance became automatic, a second skin he couldn’t shed.

That heightened state, in turn, sharpened every cue around him. A guest lingering near the front entrance too long—“acting suspiciously” in Robert’s mind—made his chest tighten and his attention narrow. The smell of beer or whiskey on a bar patron’s breath instantly transported him back to that parking lot, and his pulse would race before he could even name the memory. A dropped tray in the restaurant, a shout from the kitchen, any sudden loud noise sent a jolt through him, leaving him breathless and irritable for minutes afterward. Even at home, in the house he had shared with his wife for thirty years, Robert remained on guard. He slept poorly, starting awake at the creak of a floorboard, and when his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he reacted with a flinch that worried them both.

His occupation became a daily ordeal. As a manager, Robert was expected to greet guests warmly, to move through the lobby with ease. Instead, he found himself circling the perimeter, avoiding clusters of young men, reading hostility into casual glances. The trigger of “people acting suspiciously” now seemed to appear constantly—a guest who lingered too long at the elevator bank, a delivery driver who didn’t match the uniform. Each instance reinforced his sense that the world was unsafe, and that reinforcement tightened the loop: the more he believed people were untrustworthy, the more hypervigilant he became, and the more hypervigilant he was, the more triggers he noticed.

The humiliation lingered, too, a quiet burn beneath everything. Robert had always seen himself as competent, in control. The mugging had cracked that image, and he couldn’t stop rehearsing it—what he should have done, how he should have seen it coming. That self-critical rumination fed his mistrust of others and his constant expectation of threat. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion, and his body remained locked in a state of alarm that no logic could soothe.

What finally brought Robert to seek help was his wife’s quiet observation that he no longer seemed to live in their home—he was always scanning, always startled, never present. He was afraid that his vigilance was ruining the one relationship that still felt safe. He wanted to stop feeling like a target in his own life, to walk through a hotel lobby without his stomach clenching, to hear a sudden noise and not feel his past slam into him again. He hoped, above all, to find a way back to the ordinary world he had lost that night in the parking lot.
